title: How long does a swing take?
summary: Time a pendulum's swing, see how big swings slow it down, and compare with the small-angle formula.

steps.title: A small swing
steps.text:
A pendulum's period is the time for one full swing, there and back. For small swings it is

    T₀ = 2π √(L / g)

which is about 2.006 s for a 1 m pendulum on Earth.

Load the setup (a 5° swing with no damping) and press Run. The Summary tab shows "Period (measured)", timed from the simulation itself.

check.hint: Load the setup, then press Run.
check.success: About 2.006 s, just as the formula predicts.

steps.title: A big swing
steps.text:
Now start the pendulum at 150°, close to upside down, and run it again. Is the period still 2 s?

The setup also ticks "Keep previous runs", so the small swing stays on the plots for comparison.

check.success: About 3.5 s: large swings take noticeably longer, so the small-angle formula only holds for small angles.

steps.title: Period against amplitude
steps.text:
Sweep the starting angle to see the whole curve. The Analyze ▸ Sweep tab is set up for 5° to 175°: press Run sweep and choose "Period (measured)" in the Plot list.

Near 180° the period grows without limit. A pendulum balanced exactly upside down would wait there forever.

steps.title: What the linear model says
steps.text:
The Analyze ▸ Modes tab linearizes the pendulum about hanging straight down, θ'' ≈ −(g/L)·θ. The period of that "Swing" mode is the small-angle T₀.

Make the pendulum 4 m long (Length, in the Pendulum section) and run it. The Analyze ▸ Modes tab should now predict a period twice as long, about 4.01 s, because T₀ grows with √L.

check.success: Four times the length, twice the period.
